title: HE WAS ALLOWED TO MARRY… BUT GOD FORBADE HIM FROM TOUCHING THIS ONE WOMAN.
paragraphs: HE WAS ALLOWED TO MARRY… BUT GOD FORBADE HIM FROM TOUCHING THIS ONE WOMAN.

She wasn't his mother. She wasn't his sister. She wasn't even related to him by blood. Yet God drew a line that no desire, excuse, or family secret could erase. And the reason behind that ancient command exposes something terrifying about sin—and something breathtaking about the grace of Jesus Christ.
“A man shall not take his father's wife, nor uncover his father's nakedness.” — Deuteronomy 22:30 (ESV)
There are sins people commit in darkness because they know they are wrong.
And then there are sins people commit in broad daylight because they have convinced themselves they are right.
The second kind may be even more dangerous.
Because when a person no longer feels the need to hide, when conscience has been silenced and conviction has been replaced by clever explanations, something has already begun to die inside the soul.
Imagine a young man standing before his family.
He has made a decision.
A decision that will fracture relationships, dishonor his father, and violate a boundary God Himself established.
Perhaps someone asks him, “How could you do this?”
And perhaps he answers with the kind of argument people have been using for thousands of years.
“But she's not my real mother.”
Five words.
One excuse.
And a devastating misunderstanding of holiness.
Because in Deuteronomy 22:30, God was not merely protecting bloodlines.
He was protecting the sacred boundaries of marriage, the integrity of the family, and the moral order of a people called to belong to Him.
And what makes this command so unsettling is that it exposes a question many of us would rather avoid.
Have we ever tried to make something acceptable simply because we could find a technical excuse for doing it?
Before you answer, stay with this Scripture.
Because this is not merely a story about a forbidden relationship thousands of years ago.
It is about the frightening ability of the human heart to defend what God has forbidden.

And eventually, it leads us to a scandal in the New Testament, a grieving apostle, a church forced to confront its own compromise, and a Savior whose grace is powerful enough to redeem even the most shameful chapters of a human life.
But first, we need to understand what God actually said.
The Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 22:30 reads:
לֹא־יִקַּח אִישׁ אֶת־אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו וְלֹא יְגַלֶּה כְּנַף אָבִיו
Lo-yiqqaḥ ish et-eshet aviv, velo yegalleh kenaf aviv.
A close translation is:
“A man shall not take his father's wife, and he shall not uncover his father's covering.”
The Hebrew expression אֵשֶׁת אָבִיו (eshet aviv) means “his father's wife.”
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not limit the prohibition to the man's biological mother.
It identifies the woman by her marriage to his father.
That distinction matters.
The command includes a father's wife even when she is not the son's mother by birth.
And the final expression, כְּנַף אָבִיו (kenaf aviv), literally refers to his father's “wing,” “edge,” or “covering.”
In this context, it is figurative language connected to the father's marital and sexual rights.
This is why many English translations render the phrase as uncovering the father's nakedness, while others preserve the imagery of the father's covering.
The Hebrew imagery is not permission to speculate about a hidden ritual or mysterious spiritual mechanism.
Its meaning is grounded in the surrounding biblical laws concerning marriage, sexual boundaries, and family relationships.
Leviticus 18:8 makes the prohibition even more explicit:
“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife; it is your father's nakedness.”
God was not saying that the woman and the father were physically the same person.
He was teaching that violating the father's marriage was an offense against the intimate union and family relationship established through that marriage.
The marriage covenant mattered.
Family boundaries mattered.
Sexual conduct mattered.
And a man's desires did not give him authority to rewrite those boundaries.
This was not simply a matter of social embarrassment.
Leviticus 20:11 treated such conduct as a grave violation under Israel's covenant law, attaching a severe judicial penalty to it.
Those civil penalties belonged to ancient Israel's legal order. Christians are not authorized to enforce them today.
But the New Testament does not dismiss the underlying sexual prohibition as irrelevant.
In fact, it confronts the same kind of wrongdoing with astonishing directness.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because centuries after Moses gave that command, a Christian congregation found itself facing almost the same scandal.
The church was in Corinth.
And something deeply disturbing was happening among people who professed to follow Jesus.
Paul wrote:
“It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father's wife.” — 1 Corinthians 5:1 (ESV)
Read that again.
A man had his father's wife.
The very relationship forbidden in Deuteronomy was now being reported inside a Christian congregation.
We are not told every detail.
Scripture does not identify the woman by name, explain how the relationship began, or establish whether the man's father was still alive.
We should not invent those details.
But the central offense is unmistakable.
A man was involved in a sexual relationship with his father's wife.
And perhaps the most shocking part was not simply what the man was doing.
It was how the church was responding.
Paul continued:
“And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?” — 1 Corinthians 5:2 (ESV)
They should have been grieving.
Instead, they were proud.
Think about that.
A church that should have been brokenhearted over serious sin had somehow become comfortable enough to boast.
We do not know the exact arguments they used.
Perhaps they misunderstood Christian freedom.
Perhaps they confused tolerance with love.
Perhaps they simply refused to confront a difficult situation.
But Paul would not allow their spiritual confidence to disguise their moral failure.
And suddenly, an ancient command begins to sound painfully modern.
Because we live in a world where people can become remarkably skilled at explaining away what they do not want to surrender.
We rename things.
We soften things.
We create exceptions.
We search for voices that agree with us.
And sometimes we even use the language of grace to protect the very sins from which grace calls us to turn.
We say, “God knows my heart.”
And He does.
That is precisely why we should tremble at the thought of hiding behind religious language.
Because God sees not only our outward actions but also the motives, rationalizations, and secret compromises beneath them.
He knows when we are struggling against sin.
And He knows when we have stopped struggling because we have decided to make peace with it.
Those are not the same thing.
A wounded believer crying out for mercy is not the same as an unrepentant person demanding approval.
Jesus welcomes sinners who come to Him.
But He never tells them that sin is harmless.
And that distinction is not cruelty.
It is love.
Imagine a physician discovering a deadly infection and saying nothing because the patient might feel embarrassed.
Would that silence be compassion?
Of course not.
Love sometimes speaks the truth we desperately need, even when the truth is painful.
And this is what Paul was doing in Corinth.
He was not trying to entertain the congregation with scandal.
He was confronting a destructive situation because the holiness of the church, the seriousness of sin, and the spiritual welfare of the offender mattered.
In 1 Corinthians 5:5, Paul spoke of severe church discipline with the ultimate purpose that the man's spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.
That is a remarkable detail.
Even in a chapter filled with painful correction, salvation remained in view.
The purpose was not revenge.
It was not humiliation for public entertainment.
It was not permission for Christians to become cruel.
It was a call to take sin seriously while refusing to abandon the hope of repentance.
And here is where we need to be careful.
Because someone reading this may be carrying a story they have never told anyone.
Perhaps you crossed a sexual boundary.
Perhaps you betrayed someone who trusted you.
Perhaps you became involved in a relationship you knew was wrong.
Perhaps your family has been torn apart by adultery, secrecy, or betrayal.
Or perhaps you are the one who was wounded by another person's choices.
You may have spent years trying to make sense of what happened.
You may have heard people use Scripture to shame you for something someone else did to you.
If that is your story, hear this clearly.
Being harmed, coerced, abused, or exploited is not the same as willingly committing the wrongdoing described in these passages.
The guilt of an offender must not be transferred to a victim.
God's commands concerning sexual holiness must never be twisted into weapons against those who have suffered abuse.
The God who calls His people to purity also loves justice, truth, and the protection of the vulnerable.
And if someone used religious authority to silence your pain, their misuse of Scripture does not represent the heart of Jesus.
Christ does not need your suffering to be hidden in order for His holiness to be defended.
He is the light.
He brings hidden things into the light.
And the light of Christ exposes evil while offering mercy to those who turn to Him.
But there is another person who needs to hear this message.
The person who knows they have sinned.
The person who has been defending what they should have confessed.
The person who has spent years rehearsing excuses because admitting the truth would require an entirely different life.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you are respected at church, trusted by your family, and admired by people who have no idea what is happening behind closed doors.
But somewhere beneath the outward appearance, your conscience has been whispering.
And you have been trying not to listen.
What if the discomfort you feel while reading this is not evidence that God has abandoned you?
What if it is an invitation to stop running?
Scripture says:
“Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.” — Proverbs 28:13 (ESV)
Notice those two words.
Confesses.
Forsakes.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered the truth.
It is not simply crying because consequences have arrived.
It is not promising to change while secretly planning to continue.
Repentance involves a genuine turning of the heart toward God, a turning away from sin, and a willingness to walk in obedience.
The New Testament uses the Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance.
It refers to repentance involving a changed mind and direction, not merely a passing emotion.
And that change is not something we manufacture to purchase God's forgiveness.
It is the response of a heart being confronted by God's truth and drawn toward His mercy.
Here is the beautiful tension at the center of the Gospel.
Sin is more serious than we want to admit.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is greater than we dare to imagine.
Not because grace makes sin acceptable.
But because Christ came to save sinners.
The cross is not God pretending evil does not matter.
The cross is the place where the seriousness of sin and the astonishing love of God meet.
Jesus did not suffer, die, and rise again so that we could become comfortable with the darkness.
He came to rescue us from it.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up every secret.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not mean everyone is automatically forgiven without repentance and faith.
It means salvation is offered through Jesus Christ because of what He has accomplished, not because sinners can make themselves worthy.
And the same Savior who offers forgiveness also calls His people into a transformed life.
Paul told the Corinthians something extraordinary in the very next chapter.
After naming several patterns of unrighteous living, he wrote:
“And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11 (ESV)
Such were some of you.
Not “such must you always remain.”
Not “your worst chapter is your permanent identity.”
Not “your past is more powerful than My grace.”
Some of the people in that congregation had histories marked by serious sin.
Yet Paul could speak of them as washed, sanctified, and justified through Jesus Christ.
That is the miracle of redemption.
Not that the past never happened.
Not that consequences magically disappear.
Not that everyone you wounded must immediately trust you again.
But that a person's relationship with God can be radically changed through Christ.
Forgiveness does not erase the responsibility to tell the truth, make appropriate restitution, respect boundaries, or accept consequences.
Grace is not a shortcut around accountability.
It is the power and mercy of God that calls us into a new way of living.
And perhaps that is why the Gospel is so offensive to human pride.
Because it tells the religious person that their goodness cannot save them.
And it tells the disgraced sinner that their failure does not have to be the final word.
Both must come to the same cross.
Both need the same Savior.
Both are utterly dependent on mercy.
Now return for a moment to that man in Corinth.
Imagine the shame surrounding the congregation.
The whispers.
The damaged relationships.
The difficult conversations.
The confrontation that could no longer be postponed.
And then imagine a question hanging over everything.
Could someone involved in such a scandal ever truly change?
The Bible gives us reason to believe that genuine restoration is possible.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul urged the church to forgive, comfort, and reaffirm love toward a disciplined person who had experienced sufficient punishment.
Some interpreters believe this individual may have been the offender from 1 Corinthians 5.
Others believe the passage concerns a different incident.
Scripture does not explicitly identify them as the same person, so we should not present that connection as certain.
But the principle is unmistakable.
Church discipline must not become an excuse for endless cruelty.
Where genuine repentance is present, forgiveness, comfort, and restoration matter.
Paul warned against allowing a repentant person to become overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
That is the heart of Christian correction.
Truth without compromise.
Mercy without pretending.
Accountability without vengeance.
Restoration without denying the seriousness of what happened.
And above all, Jesus Christ at the center.
Because the Christian message is not that scandals are entertaining.
It is that the grace of God can reach people whose lives have been devastated by sin.
Not because Jesus changes the historical facts of our failures.
Not because He calls evil good.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it once was.
But because through His death and resurrection, He can forgive, cleanse, reconcile sinners to God, and begin a transformation that human effort alone cannot accomplish.
He rewrites the direction of a surrendered life.
He gives a future to people who thought they had destroyed every possibility of one.
And He teaches us that our deepest identity need not remain chained to our worst decision.
Maybe you needed to hear that today.
Maybe you have been hiding behind the words, “It's complicated.”
Maybe it really is complicated.
But complexity does not remove our responsibility to obey God.
Maybe you have been saying, “Nobody understands what I'm going through.”
Perhaps they don't.
But Jesus does.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that our great High Priest is able to sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
He understands temptation without surrendering to it.
He understands suffering without becoming unjust.
And because He is merciful, we are invited to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help in our time of need.
So bring Him the truth.
Not the edited version.
Not the version that makes you look innocent.
Not the version designed to win an argument.
The truth.
If you have sinned, confess it.
If you need to end an immoral relationship, seek the strength and appropriate support to do so.
If you have harmed someone, stop the harm and take responsibility.
If you have been abused, seek safety and trustworthy help; you are not required to place yourself back in danger to prove forgiveness.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you are exhausted from fighting temptation, do not mistake your exhaustion for defeat.
And if you have fallen, do not make your fall a permanent home.
Return to Christ.
Because the same Lord who says, “Repent,” is the Lord who gave His life so that repentant sinners might be forgiven.
And that is where this ancient command finally brings us.
Not merely to a forbidden marriage.
Not merely to a scandalous church.
Not merely to a discussion of Hebrew law.
But to the question every human heart must eventually face.
Will I allow God's Word to correct me, even when obedience costs me something I desperately want?
That is a question for the married and the unmarried.
For the pastor and the person in the back pew.
For the young believer discovering the faith and the Christian who has spent decades inside the church.
For the person who has sinned publicly and the person whose private life remains hidden.
And for those who have never thought of themselves as particularly sinful.
Because we all need more than religious information.
We need a Redeemer.
We need the cleansing mercy of Christ.
We need the Holy Spirit to reshape our desires.
We need the truth of Scripture to confront the lies we tell ourselves.
And we need a community that loves us enough to speak honestly and patiently walk with us toward maturity.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn painful Bible passages into sensational entertainment.
Not to use the failures of others as an opportunity to feel superior.
But to open the Scriptures, confront difficult truths, proclaim the Gospel, encourage repentance, and help people grow in a living relationship with Jesus Christ.

If this article has exposed something you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to respond—not to impress strangers, and not to disclose details that should remain private, but to take one honest step toward God.
You do not have to explain your private circumstances publicly.
God already knows.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not walking alone.
And if this message brought someone to your mind—a family member, a close friend, a struggling believer, or someone who has quietly drifted away from Christ—consider sharing it with them.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Because one shared message may become the beginning of a conversation someone has been afraid to start.
And one honest conversation may lead someone back to the Word of God.
There is another way you can help us continue this work.
It is not a condition for receiving His grace.
And it is not a substitute for supporting your local church or fulfilling other responsibilities God has entrusted to you.

But it can be a voluntary act of generosity—a ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the work of sharing biblical teaching, Gospel-centered articles, discipleship materials, and Christian encouragement with more people.
Scripture reminds us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity to participate in work you believe is helping people encounter His truth.
The greater purpose is discipleship.
More people reading Scripture.
More families having honest conversations about faith.
More believers learning to distinguish genuine grace from dangerous compromise.
More wounded hearts being pointed toward the compassion and truth of Jesus.
More people discovering that the Gospel is not merely a religious message to admire, but the good news of a Savior who calls us to follow Him.
The precious blood of Christ is infinitely more significant than anything we could ever contribute.
And that brings us back to where we began.
A man was forbidden to take his father's wife.
Even though she was not his mother.
Why?
Because God's boundaries were not determined merely by what a person could justify.
They were rooted in His holy design.
And when that same sin appeared in Corinth, the church was called not to celebrate it, but to mourn, confront it, and seek the offender's ultimate salvation.
That truth still matters.
We cannot call something holy simply because we desire it.
We cannot make disobedience righteous by finding someone who agrees with us.
We cannot use the word grace to silence the voice of repentance.
But neither should we imagine that a scandal places a repentant sinner beyond the mercy of Christ.
That would be another lie.
Jesus Christ is not powerless before our darkest chapters.
He is the crucified and risen Savior.
He is able to forgive.
He is able to cleanse.
He is able to restore fellowship with God.
He is able to teach a once-rebellious heart to love righteousness.
And He is worthy of our surrender.
So tonight, or whenever these words find you, ask yourself one question before you close this article.
Am I asking Jesus to transform my life, or am I asking Him to approve the life I refuse to surrender?
Do not rush past that question.
Take it into prayer.
Open the Scriptures.
Tell God the truth.
And remember the promise of 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to manufacture a beautiful confession.
There is no need to pretend you are stronger than you are.
Come to Christ with a repentant heart.
Trust in His finished work.
And follow Him into the light.
Because the most devastating thing about sin is not simply that it can destroy what we love.
It is that it can persuade us to defend the very thing destroying us.
And the most beautiful thing about Jesus is that He loves sinners enough not to leave them enslaved to what is killing them.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter—but you must stop asking the darkness to write your ending.
